Service: Shoulder Arthroscopy - Description
A shoulder arthroscopy is a minimally invasive surgical technique that may involve one or more procedures,
including the repair of shoulder components such as the rotator cuff, labrum, ligaments, or inflamed tissue or
cartilage. Through a small incision and with the aid of an arthroscope, the surgeon can thoroughly visualize the
shoulder and treat several conditions involving its structures.1-9

Procedures - Medical Necessity Criteria
Administrative Guidelines for Medical Necessity Review
Cohere Health takes an evidence-based approach to reviewing imaging and procedure requests, meaning that
sufficient clinical information must be provided at the time of submission to determine medical necessity.
Documentation must include a recent and detailed history, physical examination related to the onset or change
in symptoms, relevant lab results, prior imaging, and details of previous treatments. Advanced imaging or
procedures should be requested after a recent clinical evaluation by the treating provider, which may include
referral to a specialist.
Indications
When a specific clinical indication is not explicitly addressed in the Cohere Health medical policy, medical
necessity will be determined based on established clinical best practices, as supported by evidence-based
literature, peer-reviewed sources, professional society guidelines, and state or national recommendations,
unless otherwise directed by the health plan.
Requests submitted without clinical documentation, or those that do not align with the provided clinical
information—such as mismatched procedure, laterality, body part, or CPT code—may be denied for lack of
medical necessity due to insufficient or inconsistent clinical information.
When there are multiple diagnostic or therapeutic procedures requested simultaneously or within the past
three months, each will be reviewed independently. Clinical documentation must clearly justify all of the
following:
The medical necessity of each individual request
Why prior imaging or procedures were inconclusive, or why additional/follow-up studies are needed
How the results will impact patient management or treatment decisions
Requests involving adjacent or contiguous body parts may be considered not medically necessary if the
documentation demonstrates that the patient's primary symptoms can be adequately assessed with a single
study or procedure.

Imaging findings demonstrate ANY of the following14:
Inferior osteophytes impinging upon the rotator cuff; OR
Moderate to severe ACJ arthritis; OR
Biceps tenodesis or tenotomy and ANY of the following15:
Advanced diagnostic imaging demonstrates the presence of biceps pathology; OR
Examination findings positive for biceps pain; OR
The procedure is a debridement, and imaging studies demonstrate bony or soft tissue pathology that
correlates with symptoms and physical exam findings; OR
Loose body removal and ALL of the following11,16:
Imaging findings demonstrate the presence of a loose body; AND
Shoulder pain and mechanical symptoms; OR
Superior labrum anterior and posterior (SLAP) repair and ALL of the following11,17,18:
Examination findings consistent with symptomatic SLAP tear; AND
Imaging findings demonstrate a superior labral tear consistent with exam findings; OR
Synovectomy and ANY of the following19,20:
History or examination consistent with symptomatic synovitis; OR
Image findings demonstrate pathological synovium.
Shoulder arthroscopy is not considered appropriate if ANY of the following is TRUEB:
Arthroscopic debridement or removal of intra-articular loose body is not indicated in the presence of
Kellgren-Lawrence grade 3 or 4 osteoarthritis19,28,29; OR
Biotuberplasty, biceps sling, or superior capsular reconstruction for irreparable rotator cuff tears30-32; OR
Rotator cuff arthropathy33; OR
Rotator cuff or labral repair in the presence of active infection34; OR
Thermal capsulorrhaphy35; OR
Use of subacromial balloon spacer to treat an irreparable rotator cuff tear.36,37
The patient has completed a full course of conservative management without meaningful improvement.
Patient noncompliance, closure of therapy offices, and patient inconvenience do not constitute a failure of
conservative treatment.

Medical Evidence
Antonacci et al. (2025) conducted a systematic review to evaluate the changes in shoulder range of motion
(ROM) after arthroscopic rotator cuff surgery. In the studies included in this systematic review, ROM was
typically assessed through flexion, abduction, and internal and external rotation. Post-surgical ranges of motion,
the study found, improved gradually, accelerating at 6 months, and peaking at 12 months. These results, the
authors caution, were gleaned from ROM studies with variable patient characteristics and differing monitoring
systems, and an absence of a standardized post-surgical protocol.38
Kim et al. (2021) examined the predominance of arthroscopic distal clavicle excision procedures, specifically
those using a fluoroscopic Kirchner wire guide. The technical aspects of the procedure were described, and the
group concluded that the use of a fluoroscopic wire leads to surgical success, particularly in new orthopedic
surgeons, as the distal clavicle excision is a technically demanding procedure due to visualization difficulties. The
authors note that open distal clavicle excision remains the gold standard procedure for acromioclavicular joint
arthritis.14
Redler et al. (2019) examined the literature on treating adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder and discussed the
higher incidence of the diagnosis in diabetic patients, particularly those with long-standing, poorly controlled
disease. Hyperthyroidism was determined in studies to be an independent risk factor for developing adhesive
capsulitis. The authors preferred surgical technique post-nonsurgical interventions, including both anterior and
posterior capsular release with rotator interval release and release of the coracohumeral ligament.8
Ansok et al. (2018) reviewed optimal management strategies for glenohumeral osteoarthritis, concluding that
initial conservative treatment includes the use of viscosupplementation or corticosteroid injections. The age and
function of the affected patient should determine the necessity of operative treatment, and operative treatment
of young individuals with glenohumeral osteoarthritis remains controversial. Younger, more active patients do
benefit from non-arthroplasty techniques or procedures with minimal bone resection.39
Millett et al. (2018) examined the options for treating young, active patients with primary glenohumeral
osteoarthritis, concluding that arthroplasty may not be ideal in that population. The authors note that clinical
studies report arthroscopic approaches for procedures such as synovectomy, chondroplasty, loose body
removal, capsular release, and biceps tenodesis may improve clinical outcomes. The authors conclude that
arthroscopic management of glenohumeral osteoarthritis has numerous advantages over total shoulder
arthroplasty; however, additional larger studies are needed.19
